page.description: Guidelines for color usage in med.o products and applications

overview.aboutBody: Color is a fundamental design element that communicates meaning, enhances usability, and helps establish a consistent brand identity. In the med.o design system, colors are carefully chosen to support accessibility, ensure consistency, and reflect the system's visual language.
overview.principlesTitle: Principles of Color Usage in med.o
overview.p1Body: Colors in the med.o design system meet or exceed WCAG 2.1 AA contrast standards. This ensures content remains readable for all users, including those with visual impairments. Always verify color combinations — especially text against backgrounds — to ensure they meet contrast requirements.
overview.p2Body: Use styling hooks consistently when applying custom styles. These hooks help maintain a cohesive look across all med.o products. Avoid hardcoding colors so your design can adapt to different themes.
overview.p3Body: The med.o design system assigns specific colors to represent states such as success, error, or warning. These hooks use semantic naming, making their purpose clear. Use these predefined hooks instead of custom color values.
overview.t1Body: Our color palette is built on clean white surfaces, accented with intentional bursts of vibrant color. These highlights draw attention to key information without overwhelming the interface.
overview.t2Body: Consistent use of styling hooks allows users to quickly associate specific colors with their intended meanings.
overview.t3Body: Thoughtful color choices help direct attention, support navigation, and make it easier for users to complete tasks efficiently.
overview.t4Body: Vibrant color combinations are used sparingly to create moments of visual interest, while keeping information-dense interfaces clear and easy to understand.
overview.foundationalBody: Foundational colors give meaning to specific UI elements. Use them only for their intended purpose so users can consistently associate a color with the same meaning throughout the product.
overview.fl1Body: Full spectrum of colors without fixed assignment — usable for undefined situations.
overview.fl2Body: Colors with no semantic assignment, but commonly used by semantic hooks for UI elements.
overview.fl3Body: Used for building components and UI page elements such as backgrounds, borders, and fills. Use these colors only for their respective locations.
overview.mappedColorsLink: Learn more about mapped colors in the Tokens tab.

usage.title: When to Use Which Color
usage.intro: Always use semantic UI tokens instead of raw brand color values. This ensures future theme changes adapt automatically.
usage.semanticBody: Semantic tokens like --color-text-primary or --color-success describe intent, not the actual color value. They are the preferred choice for all UI components, as they automatically support theme changes.
usage.rawBody: Brand tokens like --color-brand-navy-500 or --color-brand-orange-800 are appropriate for themed areas and brand assets — or when no semantic equivalent exists.
usage.dontNote: Use raw tokens or hex values
usage.statesBody: Every interactive color group follows a defined state sequence: Default → Hover → Active → Disabled. Always use the corresponding token pairs — never manually calculate lighter or darker variants.
usage.surfaceBody: The system defines two primary surface levels. Level 1 is the default page background, Level 2 is the subtly elevated area. For cards and containers within these levels, use the Surface Container tokens.
usage.a11yBody: Text on colored backgrounds must meet WCAG 2.1 AA: minimum 4.5:1 contrast for normal text, 3:1 for large text (18 px+ or 14 px bold). Use --color-text-on-color on --surface_inverse or --surface_brand backgrounds.
usage.themeBody: The design system is designed for future dark mode support. Semantic tokens are the only theme-aware layer. Use only semantic tokens in component code — never direct brand or alias values.

page.description: Type system and typography guidelines for med.o products and applications

overview.scaleBody: The med.o type system covers 10 sizes — from 12 px (xs) to 60 px (6xl). Each size maps to a semantic use case: Display for hero areas, Headings for structural hierarchy, Body for reading content, and Labels for small UI elements.
overview.sansBody: DM Sans — primary sans-serif for all UI text, labels, and headings.
overview.monoBody: DM Mono — monospace for code, tokens, and technical identifiers.
overview.contextBody: Here is how type levels look in a typical page section: a Label SM marks the category, Heading XL forms the page title, Body LG provides the descriptive introduction, and Body MD carries the main content.

usage.title: Typography Guidelines
usage.intro: Always use the defined typography tokens. Hardcoded pixel values in CSS or JSX are not allowed — they break consistency and make system-wide changes difficult.
usage.headingBody: The system defines six heading levels: Display 2XL and Display XL for large hero areas, Heading XL through Heading SM for page structure. Always use the next-higher level as the parent — do not skip hierarchy levels.
usage.headingH1: H1 / Display 2XL — Page title, used once per page. Not for sub-sections.
usage.headingH2: H2 / Heading XL or LG — Primary sections of a page.
usage.headingH3: H3 / Heading MD or SM — Sub-sections, card titles, panel headings.
usage.headingH4: H4 and below — Only for densely structured content (documentation, tables).
usage.bodyBody: Body LG (18 px / 1.65) is suited for extended reading content. Body MD (16 px / 1.5) is the default for UI text and descriptions. Body SM (14 px) for help text and metadata.
usage.labelBody: Label MD (14 px / 500) for interactive elements like buttons and form fields. Label SM (12 px / 600 / Caps) for categorizing labels in tables, tags, and badges.
usage.codeBody: For inline code and code blocks, always use --font-mono (DM Mono). Combine with --text-sm and --leading-relaxed for optimal readability.
usage.lineLengthBody: Optimal line length for body text: 60–80 characters on desktop, 45–60 on mobile. Lines that are too short interrupt reading flow; lines that are too long cause eye fatigue. Use max-w-[65ch] or max-w-prose as a reference value.
usage.formattingBody: Write headings in sentence case (capitalize first letter only). Use bold sparingly — only for genuine emphasis with [font-weight:var(--weight-semibold)]. Label SM is always uppercase (text-transform: uppercase) with --tracking-widest.

page.description: 4-px grid system and spacing tokens for consistent layouts in med.o products

overview.gridBody: All spacing in the med.o design system is a multiple of 4 px. The 4-px grid is the foundation for consistent, harmonious layouts — from micro-spacing (4 px) to large section gaps (128 px).
overview.whyBody: Hardcoded pixel values create inconsistent layouts that are hard to maintain. Spacing tokens ensure that spacing stays uniform across the system and changes can be made centrally.
overview.scaleBody: 18 steps from --space-0 (0 px) to --space-32 (128 px). Each step corresponds to the next 4-px increment. The scale skips no multiples — keeping the system complete and predictable.
overview.p1Body: Use only values from the spacing scale for margins, paddings, and gaps. Magic numbers like margin: 13px create inconsistency and make system-wide adjustments difficult.
overview.p2Body: Small spacing (space-1 to space-3) for closely related elements like icon + label. Medium spacing (space-4 to space-8) for component internal padding. Large spacing (space-10+) for section separations.
overview.p3Body: Spacing tokens are independent of breakpoints — the value does not change with screen size. Responsive layouts adjust the number of columns, not the token values.
overview.anatomyBody: Here is how spacing tokens are applied in a typical card component: padding inside, gap between elements, and outer margin all follow the defined scale.

usage.title: When to use which spacing
usage.intro: Always use spacing tokens from the defined scale. Hardcoded pixel values are not allowed — they break consistency and make system-wide changes difficult.
usage.densityBody: The choice of spacing depends on information density and context.
usage.compactDesc: space-1 to space-3 (4–12 px) — Inside tight elements: icon + text gap, badge padding, chip inner spacing.
usage.defaultDesc: space-4 to space-8 (16–32 px) — Standard padding for buttons, inputs, cards, and lists.
usage.spaciousDesc: space-10 to space-32 (40–128 px) — Section separations, hero areas, page padding.
usage.do2: gap: var(--space-2) for icon + label spacing

page.description: Border radius system for brand consistency and component hierarchy in med.o

overview.principlesBody: Corner radius is a key style trait of any visual language. In the med.o design system, radius tokens define consistent rounding for all components — from sharp corners (none) to fully round pill shapes (full).
overview.p1Body: All components of a category share the same radius token. Chips and tags always get radius-sm or radius-full. Inputs always radius-md. Cards always radius-lg. This creates visual consistency without manual repetition.
overview.p2Body: Radius affects the perceived personality of a UI system. Small radii feel professional and precise; larger radii feel friendlier and more modern. The med.o system favors moderate radii for a professional aesthetic.
overview.p3Body: Larger components like modals and dialogs carry larger radii (xl, 2xl, 3xl) to emphasize their importance. Smaller containers like inputs and buttons carry moderate radii (sm, md, lg).
overview.scaleBody: 9 steps from --radius-none (0 px) to --radius-full (9999 px). Each step is intended for specific component categories.

usage.title: Which radius for which component
usage.intro: Always use radius tokens. Hardcoded border-radius values break visual consistency. Follow the recommended mappings.
usage.fullDesc: Pill buttons, avatars, progress bars, toggles

page.description: Elevation and depth perception through box shadows in med.o

overview.principlesBody: Shadows communicate depth and hierarchy in a flat UI. In the med.o design system, shadows follow the physical principle of a light source from above: light surfaces cast gentle shadows downward. Each elevation level is defined for a specific component type.
overview.p1Body: Shadows create the illusion of layers. Elements floating above content — dropdowns, tooltips — carry stronger shadows than flat content cards. This creates clear elevation hierarchies.
overview.p2Body: Stronger shadows draw attention. Use shadow-lg and shadow-xl only for elements that should be deliberately in focus — modals, dialogs, active drawers.
overview.p3Body: Do not overload a surface with shadows. Most flat cards and panels work fine with shadow-sm or no shadow at all. Shadows are an accent, not a default.
overview.elevationBody: The 7 shadow levels form a clear elevation hierarchy from near-invisible (xs) to strongly raised (2xl). shadow-inner is a special form for pressed elements such as depressed buttons or embedded inputs.

usage.title: When to use which elevation
usage.intro: Always use shadow tokens. Raw box-shadow values are not allowed. Each elevation level is intended for a specific use case.
usage.xsGuide: xs — Hover state for cards, subtle elevation
usage.smGuide: sm — Default card, flat list, default component
usage.mdGuide: md — Active cards, focus overlay, dropdown container
usage.lgGuide: lg — Dropdown menus, popovers, context menus
usage.innerGuide: inner — Pressed state, embedded inputs, inset effects
usage.dont2: box-shadow: var(--shadow-xl) for flat list items
usage.do3: No shadow on colored or image backgrounds
usage.dont3: Apply shadows on dark or image backgrounds
usage.dontNote: Raw values or wrong elevation level

page.description: Duration and easing tokens for consistent, accessible animations in med.o

overview.principlesBody: Animation and motion in the med.o design system follow a clear purpose: they provide feedback, clarify state changes, and guide attention. Motion tokens ensure that animations are consistent and accessible across the system.
overview.p1Body: Animate only when there is an informational benefit. Hover reactions, state changes on buttons, and checkbox toggles justify short animations. Decorative motion without content relevance should be avoided.
overview.p2Body: All animations must respect prefers-reduced-motion. Use @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) to disable transitions for users who prefer less motion.
overview.p3Body: Hardcoded milliseconds or cubic-bezier values are not allowed. Always use --duration-* and --ease-* tokens — this keeps all transitions in the system aligned.
overview.durationBody: 5 steps from 50 ms (instant) to 400 ms (slower). Simple state changes use the shorter steps; complex fade-in and slide animations use the longer ones.
overview.easingBody: Three easing curves for different motion characters: ease-out for elements appearing; ease-in-out for position changes; ease-spring for dynamic toggle effects.

usage.title: When and what to animate
usage.intro: Not everything needs to be animated. Motion should inform, not distract. Follow the recommendations for duration and easing.
usage.whenBody: Animate state changes (button hover/active, toggle, checkbox), appearing and disappearing UI elements (dropdown, tooltip, modal), and guided attention (notification, toast).
usage.whenNotBody: Avoid animations on layout reflows (grid changes, size transitions), continuous background motion, and elements that signal no UI function.
usage.reducedBody: Use @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) to disable all non-essential animations. Always operate components with a no-animation fallback.
